name: Slowing speech and pausing

lead: This practice involves deliberately lowering speech rate and inserting pauses, which advocates say conveys composure and authority and makes speech easier to follow.

Proponents say slower delivery and deliberate silences make speech seem more controlled and give listeners time to absorb points. It is a delivery habit that changes how you sound in the moment. No studies were located on its effect on perception.

paras: People practice slowing their pace, pausing at the end of sentences and before key points, often with recording and playback to check. It becomes natural with repeated use over time.
No risks are documented in the sources reviewed.

chain: Delivery that reads as calm and confident
angle.text: Slowing your speech and using deliberate pauses makes you sound more composed and authoritative, and gives listeners time to absorb what you say. The change is audible as soon as you apply it.

lead: Slowing speech and pausing is a delivery technique in which a person speaks at a measured pace and uses deliberate silences instead of filler words, so they come across as calm, confident and authoritative. The payoff is in presence: people use it to make their voice and delivery read as composed and self-assured, which is part of how a person is perceived alongside physical features.

Classical rhetoric counts delivery as one of the five canons, and Wikipedia's public speaking article describes it as including tone of voice, changes in pace, pauses, volume, body language and positioning.[1] Demosthenes is said to have practiced speaking while running to build breath control.[1]

In a T Nation forum post, a member advised others not to fear silence, saying that fear of silence is where verbal pauses such as 'um', 'uh' and 'like' appear, and that these fillers sound worse than silence.[2] Another T Nation thread on public speaking offers confidence tips for people who were nervous speaking.[3] Research on speech tempo and listener perception exists, including a 2001 study in the Journal of Social Psychology on speech rate, competence and social attractiveness.[4][5]
infobox: Delivery, one of Cicero's five canons[1]

paras: The technique uses unhurried pacing, pauses before and after key points, and steady breath. Public-speaking references list pace and pauses among elements of delivery, along with tone, volume and body language.[1] Practice advice in forums includes replacing filler words with silence.[2]

Speech tempo measures how many speech units are produced in a given time, and it varies with context, emotion, speaker, language and dialect. Wikipedia notes that measuring it scientifically is difficult and that units such as words per minute or syllables per second each have problems. Cruttenden (2014) gives about 4 syllables per second for English, and Arnfield and colleagues (1995) reported a range of 3.3 to 5.9 syllables per second across emotional and social contexts.[5] A radio study cited there found bulletins averaging 168 words per minute in English on the BBC and 210 in Spanish on RNE.[5]

Pauses and hesitations affect measurements: speaking rate includes them, while articulation rate excludes them.[5] Slowing speech through pauses therefore changes speaking rate without necessarily changing how fast individual words are articulated.

Fillers, also called filled pauses or hesitation markers, are sounds or words speakers use to show they are thinking but not finished, such as uh and um in American English, er and erm in British English, and like or you know among younger speakers.[6] They function in turn-taking, signalling that the speaker still wants to talk, and can indicate word searching or deeper difficulty formulating a thought.[6] A 2001 study by Fox Tree cited on Wikipedia found that hearing uh improved listeners' recognition of upcoming words while um was neither helpful nor harmful.[6] The article offers no public-speaking guidance on fillers.[6]

The 2001 Journal of Social Psychology study by Feldstein, Dohm and Crown, 'Gender and speech rate in the perception of competence and social attractiveness', hypothesised that listeners rate speakers whose global speech rates they judge similar to their own as more competent than speakers with different rates; the available summary states the hypotheses rather than the findings.[4] Wikipedia also reports that Howard Giles (1992) found a positive linear relationship between perceived tempo and perceived competence across English accents, with faster speakers rated as more competent.[5] Findings therefore differ on whether faster or slower delivery is rated more competent, and depend on listener and context.

It is discussed under voice and charisma as part of authority delivery, as a free habit that complements voice work and posture. T Nation posts present pausing as a public-speaking and presence skill rather than a physical change.[2][3]
No studies found of slowing speech and pausing as an intervention for appearance or attractiveness; related research examines speech rate and listener perception of competence.[4][5]

lore.intro: Pausing and slower speech come up in lifting and self-improvement forums as public-speaking and presence advice.[2][3]
